# Every animation was one rename away from breaking a live show


[Whatnot Engineering](https://medium.com/@whatnotengineering?source=post_page---byline--a5139b9c6bad-----------------------------------------)


9 min read


·


Just now


--


*Seth Sandler*


There’s a bug we never shipped, and it kept me up anyway. Here’s how it goes: a designer renames a property from *purchaseCount* to *purchase_count* inside an animation file. Every place our Swift code references that property is a string literal. The build stays green. Code review passes; nothing in the diff even mentions animations. And the celebration animation at the heart of our live auctions silently stops firing, in production, in front of a live audience.


Press enter or click to view image in full size


Nothing stood between us and that outcome except everyone remembering to be careful. And the strings were only the most visible tripwire. Driving our animation runtime correctly also meant knowing things the compiler never checks: call order, load timing, which properties were designer-internal and untouchable, how not to leak memory. Every engineer touching an animation had to know all of it, and every new animation was another chance to get it wrong.


If you’ve done animation work on iOS, some version of this unease is familiar. This post is the story of how we defused it: by generating the entire animation binding layer from the asset files themselves, so the compiler enforces the contract and the generated code encodes the nuance. The methodology isn’t specific to our stack, our vendor, or our app. If your code talks to any designer-owned asset through string literals and tribal knowledge, you can build this too.


## Why hand-rolled animation code collapses


Our first instinct, like every iOS team’s, was to build the animations ourselves. SwiftUI has *withAnimation* . Core Animation has *CAKeyframeAnimation* . We’d shipped complex UI before. How hard could it be?


The animation we were building wasn’t a loop. It was state-driven: it needed a user’s avatar, their name, a running count that ramps up the visuals, and different behavior depending on who’s watching. Each input changes the intro, the escalation, the outro. In native Swift, that decomposed into:


- **State explosion.** A *@State* for the image, a *@Binding* for the count, a publisher for the mode, a synchronization tangle that grew every time the design changed.
- **No iteration loop for designers.** Every easing tweak was a code change, a review, and a build. The people responsible for how the animation feels had no way to adjust it.
- **One-off everything.** Code written for one animation couldn’t be reused for the next. Every animation was hand-rolled from scratch.


The conclusion we kept circling back to: the *behavior* of an animation should live in a designer-owned tool, and engineering’s job should shrink to binding data to it.


There’s a healthy ecosystem of runtimes built on exactly that idea: Lottie for After Effects playback,[Rive](https://github.com/rive-app/rive-ios) for state-machine-driven interactive graphics, and others. We use Rive, so it’s the concrete example in this post, but everything that follows applies to any runtime where a designer-authored asset drives behavior. What sold us was the state-machine model: you don’t *play* the animation, you *drive* it. You set inputs, fire triggers, and the state machine decides what happens.


*That choice solved the design problem. It’s also where the engineering problem started.*


## The latent enemy: nuance the compiler can’t see


Out of the box, driving an animation through the runtime’s SDK looks like this:


```text
let instance = riveViewModel.riveDataBindingViewModel?.instance  let count = instance?.numberProperty(fromPath: "purchaseCount")  count?.value = 3
```


Look at what that code trusts. It trusts that “purchaseCount” exists in the asset, that it’s a number and not a bool, that no designer will ever rename it. Break any of those and you don’t get an error. You get an optional that’s silently nil, or a no-op, at runtime.


But the strings are just the visible half. The invisible half is *sequencing and lifecycle* : set that value before the asset file finishes loading asynchronously and it’s dropped on the floor. Fire a trigger before the state machine is bound and nothing happens. Touch a property the designer added for internal state-machine bookkeeping and you break transitions with no indication why. None of this is in the type system. All of it lived in heads, Slack threads, and code review comments.


That’s the actual failure mode: correctness lived in people’s memory, and forgetting failed silently. And it isn’t a problem with any one runtime; it’s the same contract gap you hit with localization keys, analytics events, or any SDK where correctness depends on strings plus folklore.


It compounds with scale. With two animation files and one engineer, you keep it all in your head. With thirty files and a whole team, every new feature starts with someone opening the design tool, hand-transcribing property names and types, and hoping they also remembered the ordering rules. There’s no spec, no contract, just string literals, tribal knowledge, and hope.


## The insight: the asset already knows everything


The turning point was realizing the asset file isn’t opaque. It’s a structured document that knows every artboard, every state machine, every property name and type it contains. All the information an engineer was transcribing by hand was sitting in the binary, machine-readable.


So: **stop writing the binding layer. Generate it from the asset.**


The methodology, in one pass:


1. **Introspect** each asset file and extract its full structure: artboards, state machines, properties, types, defaults.
2. **Generate** a typed API from that structure: a Swift class per file, a typed property per binding, an enum per artboard.
3. **Generate the proof too.** The generator knows every property and artboard, so it also emits unit tests for the bindings and snapshot tests for the rendering. Code you generate is code you can test automatically.
4. **Hide the SDK** behind a small protocol so feature code depends only on generated types, never on the runtime directly.
5. **Encode the nuance in the generated layer** : load-order handling, lifecycle management, memory hygiene, logging live in the templates once, not in every engineer’s head.
6. **Regenerate on every asset change** , so the generated code can never drift from the asset.


The compiler becomes the contract enforcer between designers and engineers: rename a property in the design tool and the next build fails at every call site that uses it. And the generated code becomes the keeper of the folklore: an engineer who has never read the runtime’s docs can’t set a property too early, can’t fire an unbound trigger, can’t leak a display link. The generated layer gives them no way to.


Here’s the same code from above, against the generated layer:


```text
viewModel.properties.purchaseCount = 3
```


Typed, non-optional, autocompleted. If it compiles, the property exists.


## Building it: the pipeline


Our runtime’s vendor ships an open-source[code generator](https://github.com/rive-app/rive-code-generator) that reads the asset files and emits stubs. Its stock templating couldn’t express what we needed: conditional output, so that a file with data bindings generates a rich API while a simple confetti loop gets a minimal shell. We forked the generator and built our templates on[Inja](https://github.com/pantor/inja) , a Jinja2-style C++ template engine with native {% if %} blocks and partials:


```text
{% if file.has_view_model %}{% include "_properties.inja" %}{% endif %}  {% if file.has_metadata %}{% include "_metadata.inja" %}{% endif %}
```


The whole pipeline runs in CI on a dedicated animation repo. Every asset file lives there, and a change to one is a pull request like any other:


Press enter or click to view image in full size


Nobody runs anything, and nobody can skip anything. The app doesn’t contain animation files or binding code at all; it consumes a versioned package, and the only way an asset becomes part of that package is by passing lint, codegen, and the generated tests. That property turned out to be load-bearing: any generator someone has to remember to run is eventually out of date, and any check that’s optional eventually gets skipped.


A few details in the pipeline earned their keep:


**Lint before code exists, fail the PR.** The generator validates assets before emitting code: embedded images must be webp and under 200 KB. A 2 MB PNG inside an animation file is now a failed check with an exact file:line: error: message, not a binary-size mystery three releases later.


**Generated code means generated tests.** Because the generator knows every property name, type, artboard, and state machine, it emits a companion test suite alongside each binding: unit tests that verify the bindings round-trip correctly, and snapshot tests that render each artboard and diff it against a reference. A designer’s visual regression or an SDK behavior change gets caught on the PR, before a package ever ships.


**Enforced instrumentation.** Logging isn’t left to feature engineers to remember. The generated layer logs state machine activity uniformly, so every animation ships with the same structured instrumentation and debugging a misbehaving animation doesn’t depend on who wired it up.


**A privacy convention for designers.** Designers use internal properties to coordinate state machines: scratch counters, transition flags. Anything prefixed with _ in the editor is excluded from generation:


```text
purchaseCount → generated → viewModel.properties.purchaseCount  _sequenceIndex → excluded → (not visible in Swift)
```


Without this, every internal scratchpad shows up in autocomplete, and someday an engineer sets one and breaks a state machine with no idea why.


**Absorb the async timing problem once.** Asset files load asynchronously, and callers set properties before the load finishes, values that a naive implementation silently drops. The generated Properties class stores plain values and flushes them all to the SDK when the file binds. Every animation gets correct pre-load behavior for free.


## Hiding the SDK entirely


The generated code conforms to one small protocol, and that protocol is the only thing feature code ever sees:


```text
@MainActor  public protocol AnimationViewModelProtocol: AnyObject {      func play(onCompletion: (() -> Void)?)      func pause()      func stop()      func reset()      var isPlaying: Bool { get }      func createSwiftUIView(isUserInteractionEnabled: Bool) -> AnyView  }
```


Feature engineers never import the runtime. That boundary bought more than cleanliness:


- **We control the API surface.** New runtime capabilities get exposed deliberately, through a template change, not discovered ad hoc in feature code.
- **SDK upgrades are invisible.** The runtime version is an implementation detail of one module.
- **Cross-cutting fixes land everywhere at once.** When we found the runtime’s display link kept ticking for offscreen animations, burning CPU on views nobody could see, we fixed it with one view modifier that pauses on scenePhase changes and disappearance, applied automatically to every generated view.
- **Hard things become one-liners.** Image properties generate named async methods, like loadAndSetAvatar(from:), that internally handle download, decode, caching, and cancellation. The call site is a single try await.

## The proof


This system now backs every animation in the Whatnot iOS app: 30+ production animation files and counting, each with generated bindings, generated unit tests, and generated snapshot tests. The most demanding is the Jumbotron: a real-time celebration that fires per-buyer during live auctions, driven by purchase count, username, a remotely-loaded avatar, and whether you’re the buyer or a spectator. The entire integration is typed property assignments and one trigger call against generated code; the engineer who built the feature never touched the animation SDK, never learned the load-order rules, and never had a string literal to get wrong. The rename-breaks-a-live-show timebomb we opened with never went off, and now it can’t. The whole class of bug is unrepresentable.


## What we’d tell you before you build one


- **Generate from the asset, or drift is guaranteed.** Any binding layer maintained by hand is a second source of truth.
- **Make generation impossible to skip.** A shared repo where CI gates every asset change beats any step someone has to remember. If an asset can reach the app without passing lint, codegen, and tests, eventually one will.
- **Put lint where the code is born.** The generator sees every asset before code exists; it’s the cheapest possible place to enforce format and size budgets.
- **Generate the tests with the code.** The generator already knows everything the tests need to assert. Emitting the test suite alongside the bindings costs a template, and it turns every asset change into a regression-checked change.
- **Budget real time for memory and lifecycle.** Display links, retain cycles, image decoding off the main thread: this is the part that bites, and none of it shows up in the demo. (We generate a per-type leak tracker as a canary.)
- **The pattern is portable.** The same repo generates Kotlin for Android today: same introspection, same lint, same generated tests, different templates. This post focused on iOS; the multi-platform story is the next one.


We’re not done: fallback views for failed loads and disk caching with a real TTL are still on the list, and both are template or pipeline changes, the quiet superpower of this architecture: fix it once, and all animations on all platforms get it in the next package.
